newsitem.title: USA: IMF urges action to reduce forex settlement risk.
newsitem.headline: IMF urges action to reduce forex settlement risk.

text.p: The IMF on Wednesday called for urgent action to reduce settlement risk in the currency market and raised the possibility of requiring dealers to set aside capital to cover their exposures.

"A disruption in this market could have serious consequences for global trade and finance and for the international banking system," International Monetary Fund staff said in an annual report on world capital markets.
Nearly $1.2 trillion is traded each day on global currency markets. Because not all trades are settled as they occur, the risk of market disruption exists.
If dealers suddenly refuse to make foreign exchange payments to a bank because of doubts about its solvency, that could set off a chain-reaction throughout the market.

"It is unclear whether the risk of a disruption in the foreign exchange market and its impact on the global banking system have been adequately priced into foreign exchange transactions," the IMF report said, citing evidence the potential of that happening may be higher than once thought.
It said that foreign exchange settlement risk could be eliminated or substantially reduced by making it possible to finalize the two payments of a transaction at the same time.
But that is easier said than done, the report said. It would require significant reforms of major domestic payment systems and continuous coordination among major central banks.
The Group of Ten industrial countries have proposed that private banks take the lead in reducing currency risk through improved settlement procedures and other measures.

The IMF report though noted that there is no firm timetable to achieving a significant reduction in such risk and said that market participants generally would like a more comprehensive and coordinated approach to the problem.

"The significant reduction of foreign exchange settlement risk...will make foreign exchange transactions more expensive," it said. "Given the highly competitive nature of the foreign exchange market, there is little hope that market participants will succeed in constructing foreign exchange settlement arrangements without supporting measures from the central banks."
IMF staff suggested that currency dealers might be required to put up capital if private sector efforts to reduce settlement risk fall short of what is needed.

"In the event that the private sector fails to make significant progress in reducing settlement risk, it may become necessary to consider the possibility that dealers be required to hold capital against their settlement exposures," they added.
